name: Suction-assisted lipoplasty (SAL)

lead: Suction-assisted lipoplasty (SAL) is conventional liposuction: a thin hollow cannula is passed through small skin incisions and connected to suction to remove localized fat. People use it to slim areas such as the chin and neck, the abdomen, flanks and thighs, and in men for chest contour and abdominal definition.

It is the baseline against which newer variants (ultrasound-, laser-, power- and VASER-assisted) are compared. A randomized trial comparing VASER-assisted lipoplasty with SAL and another comparing laser-assisted lipoplasty with SAL used SAL as the comparator, and reviews note that no newer technology had clearly shown a statistically significant advantage over it at the time.

paras: The procedure is done by a surgeon, usually with tumescent fluid (dilute anesthetic and epinephrine) infiltrated first, under local or general anesthesia. Afterward patients wear compression garments for a period and swelling settles over weeks to months.

Reported complications include bruising, swelling, contour irregularities, numbness, seroma, infection, blood clots and, rarely, organ injury, fat embolism or death. Removed fat cells do not return, but overall body fat can return after surgery, and liposuction is not a weight-loss treatment.

chain: Cannula removes subcutaneous fat cells in targeted areas
Leaner contour, sharper jawline or defined abdomen
angle.text: SAL physically removes fat from chosen areas, so the contour changes after swelling subsides. People use it for localized deposits such as submental fullness or love handles.

lead: Suction-assisted lipoplasty (SAL) is the standard, or traditional, form of liposuction. A blunt hollow cannula attached to high-powered suction removes fat from the subcutaneous layer through small incisions.[1][2] It is the most general term for liposuction and is listed in procedure manuals as suction-assisted lipectomy.[2]

For appearance, SAL reduces localized fat and sharpens contour. People pursue it for the chin and neck, the jawline, the abdomen and flanks, the thighs, and, in men, for the chest and abdominal definition. Reviews have called liposuction the most frequently performed aesthetic operation in the world.[3]
A substantial literature compares SAL with ultrasound-assisted (UAL), VASER, laser-assisted and power-assisted techniques, usually using SAL as the reference.[4][5][6]
infobox: Cannula with vacuum suction, usually with tumescent fluid

paras: In the mid-1970s Arpad and Giorgio Fischer in Rome developed a blunt cannula attached to suction, first used on the outer thighs.[2] Yves-Gerard Illouz and Fournier extended it to the whole body with cannulas of different sizes, and Illouz added a wet technique with injected fluid.[2] In the 1980s dermatologist Jeffrey Klein published the tumescent method, which permitted liposuction under local anesthesia.[2]

In the tumescent technique a large volume of dilute lidocaine and epinephrine is infiltrated into the fat, making the tissue firm and limiting bleeding.[2] A review of infiltration in SAL describes the role of the subcutaneous fluid in the procedure.[7] Abdominal technique reviews stress careful patient evaluation and informing patients of what the technique can achieve.[8]

A randomized, contralateral trial of VASER-assisted lipoplasty versus SAL in 20 women stated that no earlier comparative study had shown a statistically significant clinical improvement from a newer technology over SAL.[5] A randomized double-blind trial compared laser-assisted lipoplasty with SAL in the same patients.[6] A systematic review of ultrasound-assisted lipoplasty found little high-level evidence comparing it with SAL and no conclusive safety advantage, with low-quality evidence of less surgeon fatigue but longer operating times.[4] A review of techniques concluded vibroliposuction was safest and most precise in the authors' view, while noting liposuction is not trivial surgery.[3]

Reviews list complications of liposuction in general and note differences between UAL and SAL.[9] Serious ones include deep vein thrombosis, organ perforation, bleeding, infection and fat embolism; others include seroma, numbness, prolonged swelling, skin necrosis and lidocaine toxicity.[2] Mortality has been reported at about one per 10,000 cases, and contour deformities in about 20 percent of patients.[2]

Removed fat cells are permanently gone, but total body fat often returns to prior levels within months, and returning fat tends to accumulate in the abdomen, including visceral fat. Liposuction does not improve metabolic problems such as insulin resistance and is not a weight-loss method.[2]
A review of plastic surgery in teenagers discusses rising numbers of procedures and the role of body image, noting that puberty is a sensitive time.[10]
